Experiment on a small patch

A thick hay-and-straw mulch that works well in a drier climate can shelter slugs on cold, wet ground. Try new ideas on a manageable area before changing the whole garden. Keep what works, understand why it works, and feel free to adapt it.

GROWING TECHNIQUES - ORGANIC GROWING

Organic growing
The core ideas

Organic growing begins with a useful bit of housekeeping: keep as much plant material as possible in the garden, turn it into compost and return it to the soil.

Keep useful material in the garden
Grow
Harvest
Compost
Return to soil
Return suitable scraps and plant waste. Add outside compost when the garden cannot make enough.
Look after the ground

Use mature compost to improve the soil and replenish what crops take from it. Organic soil needs to breathe, so avoid compaction: keep feet and barrow wheels on the paths. Respect the life under your feet: don't light fires on the soil, and don't poison the ground with chemicals that you wouldn't be prepared to eat yourself.

Work with the place you have

A plant in the right soil, with correct levels of sunshine and water, will almost always succeed. Grow the crops and varieties that suit your ground - you will find this out with time and experience; every site and every plot is different. Keep a record of successes as well as failures; work with Nature to grow what is right for your garden and your garden will ultimately flourish.

Deal with the cause

Look closely before reaching for a remedy. Check moisture, roots and recent weather. Hand-pick damaging pests where practical and fit suitable crop protection: know the likely arrival times of pests in your area and net vulnerable plants before the pests arrive.

Experiment on a small patch

A thick hay-and-straw mulch that works well in a drier climate can shelter slugs on cold, wet ground. Try new ideas on a manageable area before changing the whole garden. Keep what works, understand why it works, and feel free to adapt it.

John: Into the Zone; both 35 Years videos; Why We Make Compost. Canonical organic controls.

check.text:
GROWING TECHNIQUES - BEDS AND PATHS

Beds and paths
Finger paths and leaf patterns
Borrowing from nature

Finger paths enter from one side.

A leaf pattern branches from a central path.

Finger paths are short paths that stop before the far edge, making a shape like the fingers in a hand. You gain extra growing space this way, but lose access from one edge.

A plant leaf maximises photosynthesis area with veins spreading out from a central spine. You can mimic this pattern with your paths, to maximise your growing area.

Give the paths a shape that suits the ground, then try it out with pegs and string. A clever drawing is only useful if you can work from it.

Work with sun and slope

Where the site allows, run long beds north to south so tall crops share their shade across the day. Existing buildings and drainage may matter more than compass neatness. Watch where rain collects before settling the layout.

Try the paths for size

Peg out the edges, then walk the routes with a loaded barrow. Allow room to park, turn and work beside it. Check with everyone who will use the plot; a path that suits you may be awkward for somebody else.

Sides are optional

Mounded beds need no timber and leave fewer crevices for slugs in a wet garden. Framed beds hold a flatter surface and can raise the working height. Choose what makes the plot easier to use for you.

John: Raised Beds; Sun, Drainage & Access, 00:03–05:37. Layout ideas, not scale plans.
